mainTopic: A vow forbidding benefit from someone else's property, and how שביעית (when fruit becomes ownerless) affects that vow
overview: The משנה teaches that someone under a vow not to benefit from his friend may never walk into his friend's field. He may eat fruit leaning out of it only during שביעית, when the fruit is ownerless. If the vow covered only food, he may walk in, and during שביעית he may also eat. The גמרא brings רב and שמואל: if the owner said 'these properties' before שביעית, the fruit stays forbidden even once שביעית comes. רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש say that if he said 'my properties,' the fruit becomes permitted in שביעית. The גמרא suggests they disagree about whether a person can forbid his item even after it leaves his ownership. It then attacks that idea. If anyone held this view, they should have argued about 'these properties' too. Also, a משנה about a father who forbids his son from benefiting from him seems to show that a vow can reach past ownership. That proof continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A benefit vow before and during the Sabbatical Year
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a person forbidden by vow from benefiting from his friend may not enter his friend's field. Before שביעית, he also may not eat leaning fruit. During שביעית, he may eat it.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If someone is forbidden by a vow from getting any benefit from his friend, then before the Sabbatical Year he may not go into his friend's field, and he may not eat fruit hanging over from it. During the Sabbatical Year he still may not go into the field, but he may eat the fruit of the trees that hang over.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the rule for a מודר הנאה regarding his friend's field and its fruit, comparing a regular year to שביעית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Walking into the field is always a benefit from the owner's land, so it is always forbidden. In a regular year the fruit belongs to the owner, so even fruit leaning outside the field is forbidden. In שביעית the fruit is הפקר (ownerless), so eating it is no longer benefit from the friend.

steps.title: A vow forbidding only his friend's food
steps.stepSummary: If the vow forbade only food, he may enter the field. He may not eat the fruit before שביעית, but during שביעית he may enter and eat.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he vowed not to benefit from his friend's food, then before the Sabbatical Year he may go into the field but may not eat its fruit. During the Sabbatical Year he may go in and eat.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a second case, where the vow covered only food and not every kind of benefit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since only food is forbidden, walking in the field is fine. In a regular year the fruit is the friend's food, so it is forbidden. In שביעית the fruit is ownerless, so it is not his friend's food at all, and he may eat it.

keyTerms.meaning: He made a vow
Food
Fruit or produce

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's key idea: in שביעית the fruit is ownerless, so a vow tied to the friend does not stop a person from eating it. Only things that still belong to the friend, like the land, stay forbidden.

phrases.english: If he vowed regarding food from him,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second case in the משנה, a narrower vow covering only food.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A food-only vow allows entering the field. The fruit is forbidden before שביעית and permitted during it.

steps.title: רב and שמואל: a vow before the Sabbatical Year stays in force
steps.stepSummary: רב and שמואל say that if the vow 'these properties are forbidden to you' was made before שביעית, the leaning fruit stays forbidden even after שביעית arrives. If the vow was made during שביעית, the fruit is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: רב and שמואל both say: If he said, 'These properties are forbidden to you' before the Sabbatical Year, the other may not enter the field and may not eat the leaning fruit, even after the Sabbatical Year arrives. But if he made the vow during the Sabbatical Year, the other may not enter the field, but he may eat the leaning fruit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רב and שמואל, who add a point about timing. A vow made before שביעית keeps the fruit forbidden even after שביעית begins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב and שמואל rule on a vow worded 'these properties,' which points at the fields themselves. If that vow was made before שביעית, while the owner still owned the fruit, the prohibition stays on the fruit even after it becomes ownerless. If it was made during שביעית, the fruit was already ownerless, so it is permitted.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש: the fruit becomes permitted
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש say that with the vow 'my properties are forbidden to you,' made before שביעית, the leaning fruit becomes permitted once שביעית arrives.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש both say: If he said, 'My properties are forbidden to you' before the Sabbatical Year, the other may not enter the field and may not eat the leaning fruit. Once the Sabbatical Year arrives, he still may not enter the field, but he may eat the leaning fruit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second pair of אמוראים, who rule that the fruit becomes permitted once שביעית comes, even though the vow was made earlier.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This seems to clash with רב and שמואל. For רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש, once the fruit leaves the owner's hands in שביעית, the vow no longer holds it. The vow's wording is also different here: 'my properties' rather than 'these properties.'

steps.title: Suggesting the principle behind their disagreement
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the two pairs disagree about whether a person can forbid his own item even after it leaves his ownership.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say they disagree about this? רב and שמואל hold that a person can forbid an item he owns, and it stays forbidden even after it leaves his ownership. רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש hold that a person cannot forbid an item he owns once it leaves his ownership.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to explain the argument by connecting each side to a general principle. The word 'לימא' tells us this is only a suggestion, so the גמרא may test it next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב and שמואל hold that the prohibition the owner placed on the fruit stays even after שביעית makes it ownerless. רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש hold that the prohibition ends when the fruit leaves his ownership. The question is whether the vow's power depends on ongoing ownership.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Shall we say?' A suggestion the גמרא may later reject
They disagree
A person can forbid something that is in his ownership
Even once it leaves his ownership

steps.confusionAlert: 'לימא' is not a final conclusion. It is a proposal, and the גמרא often goes on to reject it. Notice that the two pairs also used different vow wordings ('these properties' and 'my properties').
steps.whyThisMatters: The principle of אדם אוסר דבר שברשותו לכשיצא מרשותו comes up across many סוגיות about vows and prohibitions. It asks whether an owner's prohibition can outlast his ownership.

phrases.english: Shall we say that they disagree about this:
that Rav and Shmuel hold:
A person can forbid an item that is in his ownership
even for when it leaves his ownership.
phrases.notes: Here that happens when שביעית arrives and the fruit becomes ownerless.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish hold:
A person cannot forbid an item that is in his ownership
for when it leaves his ownership.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to explain the disagreement between the two pairs in steps 3 and 4 with one principle.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the disagreement between רב and שמואל and רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש really about whether a prohibition lasts after the item leaves the owner's possession?

steps.title: Does anyone really say a vow stops when the item leaves the owner?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the suggestion from step 5. If רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש really held that a vow cannot reach past ownership, they should have argued about the wording 'these properties,' and then 'my properties' would follow even more so.
steps.simpleTranslation: Can you really understand it that way? Is there anyone who says a person cannot forbid an item he owns so that it stays forbidden after it leaves his ownership? If so, let them argue about 'these properties,' and all the more so about 'my properties'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is attacking its own suggestion from step 5. It doubts that anyone holds a vow cannot reach past the owner's ownership.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The wording 'these properties' points at the actual fields, so it is the strongest case for the vow staying in force. The wording 'my properties' depends on the fields still belonging to the owner. If רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש really held that a vow cannot reach past ownership, they should have said so even about 'these properties'. Since they spoke only about 'my properties,' their reason must be the weaker wording, not a general rule about ownership.

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two wordings. 'These properties' points at the fields themselves, while 'my properties' only covers what is still his. That difference is the whole point of the challenge.

steps.kashyaTarget: The suggestion that the two pairs disagree about whether a person can forbid an item after it leaves his ownership.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש rejected that rule, they should have argued about the stronger wording 'these properties.' They chose 'my properties,' so their reason is the weaker wording.

steps.title: A משנה shows a vow can last past ownership
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adds a second challenge: a משנה teaches that a person can forbid his item even after it leaves his ownership. It begins quoting the case of a father who forbids his son from benefiting from him.
steps.simpleTranslation: And furthermore, didn't we learn that a person can forbid an item he owns even for after it leaves his ownership? As we learned: One who says to his son, 'It is קונם that you benefit from me': if the father dies, the son inherits him. But if he said 'during my life and in my death,'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second, stronger challenge from a משנה. It starts quoting a case about a father's vow against his son, and the quote continues in the next section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the father's vow said only 'benefit from me,' the son may inherit, because after death the property is no longer the father's. The משנה goes on to the case where the father said 'during my life and in my death.' That second case is the proof that a vow can reach past ownership. The text here stops in the middle of it.
